title: Till Death Do Us Part: A daughter’s account helped solve her mother’s murder in South Africa
subtitle: Ronnie Roets blamed intruders for his partner’s death. More than two years passed before police arrested him. A conversation with a social worker helped investigators establish what happened.
author: ATHENA

paragraphs.text: When police first investigated a mother’s death in Jansenville, South Africa, her partner and their daughter gave them the same account: robbers had attacked her. Later, the girl told a social worker that her father had assaulted her mother and instructed her to blame intruders. On 12 November, the High Court in Makhanda sentenced her father, Ronnie Roets, to life in prison for murder.
Roets, 45, also received three years for attempting to defeat the ends of justice. The two sentences run concurrently, according to Eastern Cape police and the South African news outlet IOL.

The woman, whom police did not name in their statement, died after Roets assaulted her at home on 23 September 2023. Police say he had accused her of having an affair. Their account offers no evidence that she had one and says nothing about whether she had previously reported abuse. What the court established was that Roets murdered her.

The next morning, the woman’s family came to the house after Roets told them she was not waking up. They found her body and police were called. The couple’s daughter was 11 at the time. Her first statement appeared to confirm her father’s story; only later did investigators learn that both accounts had come from him.

Police took further statements from the girl and the social worker. They arrested Roets on 22 April 2026, more than two and a half years after the killing. Under questioning, he acknowledged that there had been no robbery and admitted assaulting his partner, police said. Their statement does not date the social worker’s interview or explain the interval before the arrest.

South Africa’s national femicide studies show how often the identity of a woman’s killer remains uncertain. In a survey covering April 2020 to March 2021, researchers at the South African Medical Research Council examined killings of women and girls aged 14 and older at a random sample of mortuaries, then checked the cases with police investigators. In 44 percent of cases, police had not identified the perpetrator. Using statistical estimates to account for missing information, the researchers put the national toll of killings by intimate partners at about three women a day that year.

In Jansenville, Major General Thandiswa Kupiso, the district police commissioner, credited the social worker alongside the detectives who investigated the murder. The distinction matters in this case. At 11, the girl had lost one parent and depended on adults to investigate the other. When the social worker heard a different account, investigators took statements from both of them. By the time police charged Roets, they also had his own admission that there had been no intruders.
